- **Favor simplicity over cleverness — and the smallest fix that addresses the root cause.** A fix that adds new mechanisms (a helper, a wrapper, a retry layer, config) where editing an existing line suffices is overengineered and gets rejected in review. Before inventing a new shape, check how neighboring integrations already solve the same problem and match it. The same bar applies to edge cases: a narrow race or double-failure edge that self-corrects on the next cycle (or whose outcome is still correct for the user) is documented — or made observable with a log line — not engineered around with new state machines or guards.

- **Reuse the codebase's words; never coin a verb.** A name is found, not composed: before naming a function, helper, constant, status value, or table, grep for how neighbors name the same operation on the same kind of thing (`rg -n 'def \w+_<noun>\b'`, `rg -n 'def \w+_row\b'`) and pick from the verbs that come back; the search is by object, never by a list of verbs, because a list is itself a vocabulary that drifts. Dynamo row helpers are `create_ / get_ / update_ / store_ / delete_<thing>_row`. Under `integrations/`, data-function and action names come from the resource and action contracts, so there is nothing to choose. A status string is the word the API's error text uses for that state (`unconfirmed` when the 409 says "could not be confirmed"), so the row, the log line, and the error read the same. A word from one recent feature is not established vocabulary; count its uses across the repo before adopting it. Payments, ops, and distributed-systems jargon (`settle`, `claim`, `release`, `landed`, `in flight`, `ambiguous`, `reconcile`) is a coined verb here unless the grep shows it already carries that meaning in this codebase. Say what the code does in words the code already uses: `mark_<row>_succeeded`, `store_write_ids_for_replay`, `write_may_have_reached_vendor`.
- **Comments and error messages use the code's own names.** A comment names the function, status, and field exactly as the code spells them and describes the mechanism in the same verbs. A comment that introduces a second vocabulary for the thing beside it is rewritten in the code's words or deleted.

## Running code & tests
- **Tests: only `yarn test` with filters.** Never `python -m pytest` or raw `pytest`. Scopes/markers: `.claude/skills/run-scripts/guides/test.md`.
- **Ad-hoc Python: `uv run python3`.** Never raw `python3`/`python` — dependencies resolve through `uv`.

Ad-hoc handling diverges from it two ways: a placeholder stays truthy, so a required-non-null field then fails `Field may not be null` and aborts the crawl page (or an `or fallback` never fires); and a padded real value stays un-trimmed, so it splits into false duplicates against its clean twin.
.claude/knowledge/integration-gotchas.md:120:- How to handle: probe API behavior directly. For uniqueness, attempt the violating operation (POST a duplicate) and observe the vendor's response. For field presence, look for an endpoint returning historical data the seed script didn't touch. A negative API response is evidence; a sandbox snapshot is not.
.claude/knowledge/integration-gotchas.md:132:- How to handle: probe it rather than reasoning about it. Query a window whose upper bound is `now()` in UTC against records you know exist, then the same window shifted by the vendor's offset; if the first returns nothing and the second returns them, the filter is local-time. Do not assume it is uniform across the vendor: on the same host, endpoint families can differ, so confirm per family. And rule out read-back/index lag first (see the entry above) — a freshly written record invisible to *any* time window but findable by id is lag, not clock skew, and shifting the window there makes things worse.

.claude/knowledge/integration-gotchas.md:155:- When it bites: a create whose immediate read-back raises not-found invites a duplicate-creating retry (by the caller or a retry layer), or the formatted create response gets built from the empty read and drops fields. Sandboxes typically lag less than prod, so tests stay green while prod duplicates.
.claude/knowledge/integration-gotchas.md:156:- How to handle: poll the read-back with short sleeps over a bounded window; on exhaustion, format from what the create itself returned or raise a distinct "created but not yet readable — do not retry" error. Never raise `ResourceNotFoundException` there — that's the signal callers retry on.
.claude/knowledge/integration-gotchas.md:168:- How to handle: probe uniqueness early (a read scan for duplicate codes, or a create probe in a writes-safe sandbox). If non-unique, key the resource by internal id and require the internal id on writes (a `@validates_schema` that rejects code-only line items, since code to internal-id is ambiguous). Keep code as the link key only where the linked endpoint also exposes only code.
.claude/knowledge/integration-gotchas.md:170:## "lines_changes"-style write APIs: UPDATE needs the existing line id; ADD duplicates
.claude/knowledge/integration-gotchas.md:172:- Some vendors express order/receipt line edits as a `lines_changes: [{type, ...}]` array. `type:"ADD"` always appends a new line, so using it for an update accumulates quantity (set qty 1 on an existing-qty-1 line and the read-back shows 2) instead of replacing.
.claude/knowledge/integration-gotchas.md:197:- How to handle: implement re-auth-on-401 in the request helper (byrd is the exemplar) — on a 401, call `refresh_integration_secret()` (a full re-login with the stored creds, since there's usually no refresh endpoint), `update_integration_secret(...)` to persist the new token, and retry the request ONCE inline (not a recursive call — bound it to one retry). Then ask the vendor for a dedicated API credential that doesn't share the single-active-token slot with interactive UI logins; re-auth-on-401 keeps our sync alive but revokes the customer's UI session each time it fires, so it's a mitigation, not a cure.
.claude/knowledge/integration-gotchas.md:239:- How to handle: confirm the failure signature actually appears in prod telemetry before shipping, test the fix against several differently-configured live connections, and prefer fallback-on-error (keep the old request shape, retry with the new one on the specific failure) over unconditional request changes.
.claude/knowledge/integration-gotchas.md:263:- When it bites: mapping that response to invalid credentials flags the whole connection broken over one endpoint, alerting the customer for nothing; raising `NotImplementedError` instead disables the resource for every connection, because `is_implemented` reads the method source for that raise.
.claude/knowledge/integration-gotchas.md:269:- When it doesn't: the permission validator only runs for an integration whose class source calls `self.create_permissions_exception(...)` — that is exactly what `BaseIntegration.raises_permissions_exceptions()` scans the source for, and at install the validation job is only enqueued when it returns true. An integration that never raises a permissions exception never enters the validator, so `in_perm_validator()` is never true for it and the unguarded stored lookup cannot raise. A reviewer flagging the missing guard is right in general and wrong for such an integration.
.claude/knowledge/integration-gotchas.md:299:- When it bites: a retry loop or sleep that is harmless in a crawl (60s waiting out a vendor transient) holds the customer's request open for the whole wait, and stacked retries can push it past gateway timeouts, so the customer gets a 504 with the write's outcome unknown.
.claude/knowledge/integration-gotchas.md:300:- How to handle: keep write-path waits to seconds (a short bounded read-back poll is fine); surface a vendor transient as an error the caller can retry rather than sleeping through it.
.claude/knowledge/integration-gotchas.md:324:- How to handle: make the sweep unreachable unless the pass was complete. Have `store_<resource>_page_token` return False so every pass starts at page 1, and carry a flag for every point in the pass where you know you failed to read something — a vendor error that cost a record, a prefetch that didn't finish — then skip the sweep (logging why) if it is set at the end. Skipping turns a silent wipe into stale-but-correct data, which is the recoverable failure; a stale record can be fixed by the next clean pass, an overwritten one cannot.
.claude/knowledge/integration-gotchas.md:325:- Lead with the flags, but keep a "too many records went unseen" ratio behind them as the backstop. The flags are precise and name their own cause; the ratio needs a threshold nobody can source and fires late, but it is the only thing that catches a source truncating cleanly with no error at all. Order them so the log line reports the precise cause when there is one.
.claude/knowledge/integration-gotchas.md:367:- How to handle: check which set the offset counts. Short pages possible mid-stream → advance by the limit and treat only an empty page as the end. Offset counts the returned rows and the response carries a trustworthy total/hasNext → advance by rows returned and stop on the total or when `hasNext` is false. Either way, pin an explicit, unique sort key on every paginated query. When one emitted item aggregates rows that can straddle a page boundary, hold the aggregate a full page's last rows started until the next page confirms it complete — pages submitted independently can land out of order, so a partial total emitted first can stick while the complete one is dropped as a no-change duplicate. The same determinism rule applies client-side: anything a stored page token indexes into (sku chunks, id batches) must be rebuilt identically across processes — sort before chunking, since a Python `set`'s iteration order changes between runs, so a resumed crawl would rebuild different chunks and pull a different slice.
.claude/knowledge/integration-gotchas.md:390:- When it bites: the second line raises `Duplicate product_id` in order validation and wedges the whole crawl page, so every order on it stops syncing, not just the affected one. It usually shows up in prod long after tests pass, since sandbox orders rarely carry the split.
.claude/knowledge/integration-gotchas.md:417:## A read that consumes what it returns: check for an "already sent" flag before trusting a list endpoint
.claude/knowledge/integration-gotchas.md:419:- Some WMS and ERP APIs treat their outbound endpoints as a queue rather than a query. The call returns only the records that have not been collected yet and marks them collected as a side effect, so the first call looks perfect and every call after it returns zero rows. JDA / Blue Yonder does this with an `uploaded` flag on order and pre-advice extracts; the same shape shows up wherever a vendor thinks of the API as a delivery mechanism instead of a view.
.claude/knowledge/integration-gotchas.md:428:- An id-looking name is not evidence. A "tag id" on a warehouse inventory row turned out to identify a physical tag, not a row, and repeated across locations: 287 rows carried only 254 distinct values, 26 of them duplicated. A separate `key` field was the actual unique row id.
.claude/knowledge/integration-gotchas.md:458:- How to handle: build write bodies from the vendor's own documented **request** example, never from a read response, and treat the two spellings as independent facts. After the first successful create of each resource, re-read the record and diff what you sent against what came back — a green create is not evidence the value landed. Where a read-back endpoint exists, one paired probe (correct key vs suspect key) settles it in a minute.
.claude/knowledge/integration-gotchas.md:474:- The framework's default write bodies use literal values (`sku`, `"123"`), which is fine until the vendor enforces uniqueness on that key. The first run creates the record and passes; every run afterwards fails on a duplicate, including CI.
.claude/knowledge/integration-gotchas.md:475:- When it bites: the failure looks like a code regression rather than a fixture problem, and on a vendor with no delete endpoint the polluting record can never be cleaned up. .claude/references/integration-patterns.md:6:This file is the canonical pattern reference for integration subagents (`integration-api-validator`, `integration-function-writer`, `integration-reviewer`). Subagents start with clean context and **do not** auto-load the project CLAUDE.md, so this file duplicates the rules subagents need.
.claude/references/integration-patterns.md:67:3. **Re-read the spec.** Does the docs section actually claim this field exists? In what state? Are there required headers, query params, or body flags that change response shape?
.claude/references/integration-patterns.md:72:Only **after** these steps, and only with notes documenting what you found, may you reach for: `.get()`, `IntegrationNotImplemented`, custom validation, validator-disable flags, or test modifications.
.claude/references/integration-patterns.md:78:- **Disabling a validator flag** (e.g., setting a Marshmallow field's `validate` to a no-op, lowering strictness, switching `Strict()` to `Loose()`). Validators exist to catch source-side malformations before they reach customers. Disabling without investigation hides real data issues.
.claude/references/integration-patterns.md:110:Reviewer enforces: any of `IntegrationNotImplemented`, `.get(...)` with default, custom validator, validator-disable, or non-obvious source-field choice **must** have a corresponding entry in `api-summary.md` "Field-mapping decisions." Missing rationale → `[BLOCK]`. Rationale present but thin (e.g., "couldn't find it") → `APPROVE_WITH_NOTES` flagging that the user should sanity-check.
.claude/references/integration-patterns.md:126:| `additional_fields` | Default to `{}`. Populate for a field a customer has explicitly requested, or for a deliberate vendor-specific extra that no canonical field can carry and that downstream behavior needs (e.g. a source attribute a write path must read back) — rationale recorded in `api-summary.md` "Field-mapping decisions", **naming the requesting customer/org when the field was customer-requested**. An entry with no recorded requester reads as unrequested and risks removal in a later cost or coverage cleanup. Never for data that has a canonical slot. |
.claude/references/integration-patterns.md:136:When a list endpoint returns multiple rows that share a primary identifier (`sku`, `order_id`, `product_id`), the writer's first instinct is often "dedupe these — they're duplicates of the same record." **Look at what differentiates the rows before flattening.** If they share the primary identifier but differ on a secondary one (`batch_name`, `lot_id`, `serial_number`, `bin_location`, `variant_id`, `line_id`), that secondary identifier is signal that the rows are a **decomposition** of one canonical record — not duplicates — and the secondary structure usually maps to a canonical sub-collection.
.claude/references/integration-patterns.md:145:| `order_id` | `line_id` / `package_id` | Line items or packages, not duplicate orders. Aggregate up by `order_id`, keep the inner rows as `line_items` / `packages`. |
.claude/references/integration-patterns.md:177:| Raise, don't `assert` | Runtime error paths raise `PokedexException` (or the typed `create_*` helpers), never `assert`. Asserts strip under `python -O` and carry no status code or origin for the error surface. `assert` belongs in tests only. **Advisory on existing code; flag in new builds.** |
.claude/references/integration-patterns.md:187:| De-duplicate shared rationale | When the same comment applies to multiple fields (e.g., "proto3 omits zero-valued fields, so this is absent on no-records responses" repeated on five fields), put the comment ONCE — at the function header, above the relevant block, or as a module-level note near the parsing helper that handles it. Repeating the same rationale on every field is noise that obscures the per-field comments that *are* unique. |
.claude/references/integration-patterns.md:190:| Comments are ≤2 lines | A comment longer than two lines is almost always restating the code or describing what (not why). Keep to one short line ideally; two when the *why* needs a clause. Multi-paragraph or 5+ line comment blocks are forbidden unless the situation genuinely requires it (unusual vendor quirk that takes a paragraph to explain, with a date / observation). Reviewer flags >2 lines as `APPROVE_WITH_NOTES` and asks: can this be one line, or moved to `api-summary.md` "Field-mapping decisions"? |

- How to handle: route every unbounded section through one small helper — `extract_list(parent, child_key)` — that returns `[]` when the parent is falsy/absent or the key is missing, wraps a lone dict in `[dict]`, and passes a list through. Apply it at every repeated level (lines, packs, pack-lines, references); guard only structural wrapper nodes, never data fields (or you mask genuinely-missing-field bugs).

## A record just created may not be readable yet — treat read-back lag as normal

- Vendors with async write pipelines accept a create and then answer the detail/list read with an empty result for seconds to minutes — often as `200` with "no records" / `items: []`, not a 404. Presence of the record's id field in the read body, not the create's status code, is the readiness signal.
- When it bites: a create whose immediate read-back raises not-found invites a duplicate-creating retry (by the caller or a retry layer), or the formatted create response gets built from the empty read and drops fields. Sandboxes typically lag less than prod, so tests stay green while prod duplicates.
- How to handle: poll the read-back with short sleeps over a bounded window; on exhaustion, format from what the create itself returned or raise a distinct "created but not yet readable — do not retry" error. Never raise `ResourceNotFoundException` there — that's the signal callers retry on.

- How to handle: route every unbounded section through one small helper — `extract_list(parent, child_key)` — that returns `[]` when the parent is falsy/absent or the key is missing, wraps a lone dict in `[dict]`, and passes a list through. Apply it at every repeated level (lines, packs, pack-lines, references); guard only structural wrapper nodes, never data fields (or you mask genuinely-missing-field bugs).

## A record just created may not be readable yet — treat read-back lag as normal

- Vendors with async write pipelines accept a create and then answer the detail/list read with an empty result for seconds to minutes — often as `200` with "no records" / `items: []`, not a 404. Presence of the record's id field in the read body, not the create's status code, is the readiness signal.
- When it bites: a create whose immediate read-back raises not-found invites a duplicate-creating retry (by the caller or a retry layer), or the formatted create response gets built from the empty read and drops fields. Sandboxes typically lag less than prod, so tests stay green while prod duplicates.
- How to handle: poll the read-back with short sleeps over a bounded window; on exhaustion, format from what the create itself returned or raise a distinct "created but not yet readable — do not retry" error. Never raise `ResourceNotFoundException` there — that's the signal callers retry on.

    multi = re.search(r"from utils\.exceptions import \(\n(.*?)\)", src, re.S)

    if len(line) > 89:
        inner = ""
        for name in names:

    return src.replace(single.group(0), line)

124:| `created_date` / `updated_date` | Pull from source when present. **When the vendor exposes only one of them** (creation-only systems, append-only logs, audit-trail revisions, single revision timestamp like `time` / `last_modified`), **set the missing one equal to the present one**. 127:| `IntegrationNotImplemented` | Use **only** when a field is structurally absent from the integration's API in **both directions**: no read endpoint exposes it AND no write endpoint accepts it. 136:When a list endpoint returns multiple rows that share a primary identifier (`sku`, `order_id`, `product_id`), the writer's first instinct is often "dedupe these — they're duplicates of the same record." **Look at what differentiates the rows before flattening.** If they share the primary identifier but differ on a secondary one (`batch_name`, `lot_id`, `serial_number`, `bin_location`, `variant_id`, `line_id`), that secondary identifier is signal that the rows are a **decomposition** of one canonical record — not duplicates — and the secondary structure usually maps to a canonical sub-collection.

163:- **No `.get()` in initial implementation — on vendor-response reads.** Loud failures are how we discover real API behavior. 176:| Comments | **Default is no comment** — one exists only when the change isn't obvious from the code, and a comment restating the code, a name, or the raise beside it gets deleted, not polished. content.content:
#### Additional rules

- **Format functions are module-level free functions by default.** Define on the class only when the body actually reads `self.X` (e.g., `self.connection_id`, `self.integration_secret`). Method-on-class without `self` usage is dead encapsulation — hoist it. **Advisory in new code.**
- **Format functions make no vendor calls.** A `format_*` only reshapes the record it is given. Fetch anything extra (a lookup, a detail call, a follow-up page) in the `get_*` / `create_*` / `update_*` / `cancel_*` method and pass it in, even if that duplicates the fetch across callers. → `APPROVE_WITH_NOTES`.
- **URL paths declared inline at the request call site.** Write `self.<name>_request("/orders", method="GET", params=...)`, not `ORDERS_PATH = "/orders"` at file top followed by `self.<name>_request(ORDERS_PATH, ...)`. Paths are usage-specific; abstracting them adds indirection without reuse. **Advisory in new code.**
- **Constants live at the narrowest scope that holds all their callers.** Three placements, applied based on usage:
  - **Used by exactly one function** → inside the function body, as the first thing before any logic. This is the default for status maps, type maps, label dicts, lookup tables that one `format_*` consumes. Hoisting them above the function is dead reach.
  - **Used by 2+ functions for the same resource** → directly above the first `format_*` that consumes them, below the class.
  - **Used across resources** → module-level at file top (base URL, api version, page-size defaults, anything the integration class itself references).
  - The "above the class" placement is for the middle case only. **A single-caller `STATUS_MAP` at module scope is a `[BLOCK]`** — narrow it to function scope.
- **Request-helper cluster stays together, in the class.** `<name>_auth` / login / token-refresh / signing helpers live directly with `<name>_request` as **class methods** — even when they don't read `self`. This is the one documented exception to "hoist stateless helpers to module level": auth stays together, in the class, around the request helper. Don't intermix them with the framework install/identity defaults (a separate cluster above), and don't drop them to module level below the class.
- **Helper placement — cluster by use site.** A class-level helper used by one data method sits **directly above that method** (e.g. a custom `get_inbound_shipment_by_id` above `get_inbound_shipments`). A helper used by several sits directly above the **first** method that calls it. Don't park helpers at the bottom of the class or far from their caller.
- **Module-level helpers come after the formats, and only when shared.** Inline a one-off transform at its call site; extract a module-level helper only once it is genuinely used in **2+ places**. When extracted, it lives at the very bottom of the file, **after every `format_*` function** — never before or interleaved with them. (`format_*` are themselves module-level by the rule above; the order at file bottom is formats first, then any other helpers.)
- **No raise-only method stubs for unsupported flows.** An integration never ships a data or write method whose body only raises. Omit the method entirely — the framework's `is_implemented` treats an absent method and a raise-only body identically, so the stub is dead lines that read as intent. When the vendor's API does support the flow, implement it rather than stubbing it.

#### Reviewer enforcement (new builds + new functions only — skip on existing-function edits)

- `me` / `safe_me` placed after `<name>_request` instead of with `get_integration_secret` → `APPROVE_WITH_NOTES`. They are framework-default identity methods, not implementation details of the request helper.
- Class body section ordering deviates from the four-section sequence above → `APPROVE_WITH_NOTES` with the recommended order.
- **Methods grouped by action instead of resource** (all `get_*` methods together followed by all `create_*` together) → `[BLOCK]` on new builds. The exemplars are uniform on this; the canonical shape is each resource's gets and writes adjacent. Pre-existing integrations with action-grouped layouts are grandfathered — don't refactor.
- `format_*` placed above the class definition (rather than at file bottom) → `APPROVE_WITH_NOTES`.
- `format_*` order at file bottom doesn't mirror the resource-cluster order in the class → `APPROVE_WITH_NOTES`. `format_order` should appear in the same relative position at the bottom as the order cluster does in the class.
- `format_*` defined on the class without using `self` → `APPROVE_WITH_NOTES` (hoist to module-level).
- URL paths extracted as module-level constants → `APPROVE_WITH_NOTES`.
- **Single-caller constant defined at module / class scope instead of inside its caller → `[BLOCK]`.** Status maps, type maps, label dicts, and lookup tables consumed by exactly one function belong in that function. Check by grepping for the constant name — if there's one caller, it's a BLOCK; the narrower scope is the right one. (Two-or-more-caller constants stay above the function per the placement rule.)
- Multi-resource-shared constant placed above one function's `format_*` instead of at module scope → `APPROVE_WITH_NOTES`.
- `<name>_auth` / login / token-refresh helpers placed away from `<name>_request` (e.g., at the bottom of the class, or up with the framework defaults) → `APPROVE_WITH_NOTES`.
- An auth helper defined at **module level** (below the class) instead of as a class method in the request-helper cluster → `[BLOCK]` on new builds. Auth helpers stay in the class.
- A `*_schema` not placed **directly above the write it parameterizes** (all schemas grouped at the cluster top, or a schema separated from its `create_*` / `update_*` by the gets) → `[BLOCK]` on new builds. Pair each schema with its write.
- A class-level helper parked away from its caller (bottom of the class, or well above the first method that uses it) → `APPROVE_WITH_NOTES`.
- A module-level helper defined **before or among** the `format_*` functions → `APPROVE_WITH_NOTES` (move it below every format).
- A stateless transform extracted to a module-level helper with **exactly one caller** → `APPROVE_WITH_NOTES` (inline it; extract only at 2+ callers).
- A raise-only method stub for an unsupported flow left in `integration.py` → `[BLOCK]` on new builds (omit the method, or implement the flow when the vendor supports it).
- **Field-mapping decision recorded for a resource without consulting the vendor's write spec for that resource** (when a write spec exists — vendor documents `create_<resource>` / `POST /<resource>`) → `APPROVE_WITH_NOTES` requesting the writer cross-reference write spec to confirm ambiguous reads. `[BLOCK]` if a `Field-mapping decisions` entry shows the writer chose a non-obvious read-side mapping AND the vendor's write spec contradicts it.

## Reviewer checklist (literal pass/fail)

For each `format_*` function the function-writer touched:

- [ ] No `.get()` calls (or each `.get()` has an explanatory comment about the observed missing field)
- [ ] No `trackstar_tags` assignment
- [ ] `additional_fields` is `{}` unless customer-specified
- [ ] No `IntegrationNotImplemented` used as fallback for present-but-null values
- [ ] No `x = data.get(y, IntegrationNotImplemented)` patterns
- [ ] No `x = y or IntegrationNotImplemented` patterns
- [ ] **Write-accepted-but-read-absent fields use `None`, not `IntegrationNotImplemented`.** If the vendor accepts a field on `create_*` / `update_*` (whether or not the integration implements writes yet) but doesn't echo it on the corresponding read, the read path sets `None` with a comment naming the asymmetry — not `IntegrationNotImplemented`. The vendor contract determines the absence value, not the integration's current method coverage. Check candidates: `unit_price`, `discount_amount`, `currency`, `note`, `b2b`, write-only metadata fields. Exception: a canonical `List`/`Dict` field whose schema rejects `None` (its `not_implemented_default` is `[]`/`{}`, so `allow_none` never auto-enables) takes `IntegrationNotImplemented` on the read side even when a write accepts it — with the asymmetry recorded in `api-summary.md`. → `[BLOCK]` when violated.
- [ ] **No `[]` as an absence value on structural-decomposition fields when the parent has data.** Use the vendor's per-element breakdown, or mirror the parent collection to the **single** child (canonical: `list(per_package_lines.values()) or shipment_line_items` — see shipbob). → `[BLOCK]` for an empty single-package `line_items` while the parent has data, and for an invented allocation. Exception: a vendor exposing **multiple** packages with no per-package breakdown correctly leaves every package's `line_items` empty (a fabricated split double-counts against the cross-package quantity validation), with the gap recorded in `api-summary.md`. Carve-out: event-stream collections like `inbound.receipts` are NOT structural decompositions; `receipts = []` is the correct starting state until items are received (see Inbound receipts decision tree).
- [ ] `created_date` / `updated_date` shape correct: both pulled when present; **missing one set equal to the present one** when vendor exposes only one (don't omit `created_date` while keeping `updated_date` — the pipeline backfilling `EPOCH` on the omitted side mislabels historical records as 1970); both omitted only when neither is sourceable. Never synthesized from `now()` or hardcoded dates on a read path (a `create_*` write originating the record may stamp `now()` as the true origin timestamp when the vendor echoes none — see the dates row above). → `[BLOCK]` when `created_date` is omitted while `updated_date` is set, or when either is synthesized on a read path. (The pipeline auto-copies `created_date` to a missing `updated_date`, so the integration may legitimately set only `created_date`; the inverse — only `updated_date` — is the failure case.)
- [ ] String/datetime fields don't have `or None` suffix
- [ ] No list/dict comprehensions in transformation logic
- [ ] No `logger.info` / `print` calls in integration code except carrier (carrier may use them at major async checkpoints; `logger.warning` / `logger.error` for genuinely surprising states is fine in any type)
- [ ] No docstrings
- [ ] Comments are lowercase, ~5-10 words, explain WHY
- [ ] **Comments pass the one-read test — plain English, no noun-stacks / arrow-chains / framework vocabulary.** Clarity wins over brevity; don't flag a clear comment just for running a little long.
- [ ] Comments ≤2 lines (one preferred). Multi-paragraph or 5+ line blocks only for genuinely complex situations.
- [ ] **No observation dates, customer orgs, or source-integration attribution in code comments.** Present-tense WHY only; rich rationale lives in `api-summary.md` "Field-mapping decisions" — not in the code.
- [ ] **Comments are self-contained — no references to `api-summary.md` or other gitignored files.** Inline the relevant context.
- [ ] **No doctrine vocabulary or authoring-agent attribution in code comments.** No `# tier-3 pattern`, `# per the warehouse decision tree`, `# canonical exemplar`, `# Claude/AI suggested`, `# config-driven`, etc. Comments describe local behavior, not the doctrine bucket or who wrote it.
- [ ] **`logger.warning` / `logger.error` produces actionable signal, not decoration.** A warn followed by a silent default (`logger.warning(...); value = "other"`) is decoration; pick raise-or-cast and document the choice. Warn that's logged-and-ignored with no follow-up → `[BLOCK]`. Warn paired with a default-fallback → `APPROVE_WITH_NOTES` to pick one.
- [ ] **No duplicated rationale.** If the same comment ("proto3 omits zero values", "vendor returns null for blocked-state orders", etc.) applies to multiple fields, it appears ONCE — at the function header or above the relevant block — not on every field.
- [ ] Constants live at the narrowest scope that holds all callers: single-caller constants (e.g., a one-`format_*` `STATUS_MAP`) defined inside the function body; multi-function-same-resource constants above the first consumer; cross-resource constants at module top. Single-caller constant at module / class scope → `[BLOCK]`.
- [ ] No leading-underscore "private" names — methods (`_helper()`), attributes (`self._cache`), or locals (`_tmp`). Underscore privacy isn't enforced and isn't a convention this codebase uses. A class helper needing `self` → plain method (no underscore); not needing `self` → module-level function; used once → inline. **Advisory in new integrations; ignored in existing-integration edits** (dunders like `__init__` exempt).
- [ ] `page_token` default declared inline in the function signature, not via a `page_token=None` + `if page_token is None: page_token = ...` reset (unless the default genuinely depends on runtime state — exception documented in a comment)
- [ ] A function that splits the crawl range by date returns the finished window as `next_start` (tz-aware UTC, whole seconds, `start < next_start <= end`, `next_token=None`) instead of carrying the next window's start in the page token, and the resource stores crawl params. Lookbacks live in `crawl_start_overlap_minutes`, not in the function.
- [ ] No multi-line value expressions inside dict / kwargs literals — conditionals, `any()`/`all()` over iterables, multi-step transforms get hoisted to named variables above the constructor. Trivial inline ternaries and `.get(field, default)` are fine; the rule applies once the value wraps a line or scans an iterable. **Advisory (`APPROVE_WITH_NOTES`) on new builds.**
- [ ] **Every field in the API spec is represented.** A field present in the vendor's spec/OpenAPI but absent from `format_*` is a `[BLOCK]` finding, even if the sandbox sample didn't return it. Verify by reading the spec section in `api-summary.md` and diffing against the implementation.

For ID strategy:

- [ ] If `id` maps to a non-internal-ID source field (SKU, order_number, external reference), there's a documented uniqueness probe in `api-summary.md` "Field-mapping decisions" with date + operation + observed result. Missing probe → `[BLOCK]`.
- [ ] `ignore_link_tests()` is NOT overridden as a shortcut to silence failing link tests. Override only if the source data model genuinely doesn't link the resource pair, with an explanation in `api-summary.md`. Override-without-rationale → `[BLOCK]`.

import pickle

from config import PROXY_REQUESTS_BUCKET

from transports import FtpClient, SftpClient  # noqa: F401
from utils.boto import s3
from utils.exceptions import PokedexException
from utils.lambda_util import LambdaContextManager


def handler(event, context):
    with LambdaContextManager(event, context) as ctx:
        try:
            result = getattr(ctx.client, ctx.method)(*ctx.args, **ctx.kwargs)
            response = {"ok": result}
        except PokedexException as e:
            response = {
                "error": {
                    "message": e.message,
                    "status_code": e.status_code,
                    "origin": e.origin,
                }
            }

        response_key = ctx.request_key.replace(".req.pkl", ".resp.pkl")
        s3.Object(PROXY_REQUESTS_BUCKET, response_key).put(Body=pickle.dumps(response))

**Meta / framework (not vendor resources, but accepted resource-style flags):**
```bash
--install                       # the install test
--info
--generate                      # the sandbox generate test
--openapi                       # the openapi test
--cleanup                       # @pytest.mark.cleanup tests
```

## Operation Filters

```bash
--gets                          # Only get_resource tests
--writes                        # Only write_resource tests
```

## Special Filters

```bash
--perm                          # get_resource tests without connection
--passthrough                   # Passthrough tests only
--skip-retrieval                # Skip retrieval tests only
--only                          # Only tests marked with @pytest.mark.only
```

## Other Flags

| Flag | Description | Default |
|------|-------------|---------|
| `-k <pattern>` | Filter by integration name or test name (see below) | - |
| `--pdb` | Open debugger on failure (interactive, runs serially) | false |
| `--serial` | Run tests serially | false (parallel) |
| `-n <num>` | Number of parallel workers | cores, 32 for an integration run in CI, capped at the test file count when `-k` names test files |
| `-h, --help` | Show help | - |

## How filters combine

- Type filters OR together. Resource filters OR together.
- Type, resource and operation AND together.

Example: `--wms --gets --orders` means type is WMS, AND operation is gets, AND resource is orders.

## How `-k` picks tests

1. An exact integration name (`-k deposco`) resolves to that integration's test file.
2. Otherwise, every test file whose name contains the value, ignoring `-` and `_`, is selected: `-k exten` picks extensiv-3pl-central, `-k ship` picks every file with "ship" in its name (shipstation, cybership, ...).
3. A value that matches no file name (`-k test_get_inventory`) becomes a pytest keyword filter over `test/integrations test/transports`. It matches test names, so it usually selects tests from many files.

Several `-k` flags OR together: `yarn test -k deposco -k shipbob`.

## Serial vs parallel

Tests run serially when `-k` resolves to a single test file, or with `--pdb` or `--serial`.

- An integration run splits work by file (`--dist=loadfile`), because the tests in one integration's file share a connection and run in a set order.
- A run that touches nothing under `test/integrations` (`api`, `celery`, `lambda`, `utils`, `transports`, `nonints`) splits by test (`--dist=load`).
- Workers: an integration run gets one per core locally and 32 in CI, since it waits on vendor responses rather than the CPU. A non-integration run gets one per core.
- When `-k` names test files, the worker count is capped at the number of files: `-k deposco -k shipbob` runs two workers, `-k deposco` alone runs serially. A keyword filter (step 3 above) runs at the default count with no cap.
- `-n` overrides the count, still capped at the file count when `-k` names test files.

## Examples

```bash
yarn test -k shopify                    # All shopify integration tests (serial, one file)
yarn test -k deposco --orders --gets    # Deposco order get tests
yarn test -k <name> --perm              # Perm validator test for one integration
yarn test -k deposco -k shipbob         # two files, two workers, no flag needed
yarn test -k "test_get_inventory"       # Tests matching pattern, across every integration
yarn test --wms --gets --orders         # WMS order get tests
yarn test --cart --freight              # Cart OR freight tests
yarn test integrations --cart --writes  # Cart write tests
yarn test --only                        # Only @pytest.mark.only tests

content.text:
`WriteNotReturnedException` is now raised in 19 integrations when a write's read-back runs out of time. The knowledge files tell future integrations to do the same. The changes aren't committed yet.

**Tests:** I ran the write tests for all 19 integrations: 91 passed, 2 xfailed, 199 skipped, and 1 failed. The failure was shipfusion `test_create_product`. The sandbox didn't return the new product within 20s, so the new exception fired. That's exactly the lag this ticket is about. It passed when I reran it.

**Where it's used:** bigcommerce, canary7, controlport, deposco, i-fulfilment, logicpod, logiwa, logiwa-io, masonhub, quiet, shipfusion, shiphero, shipmonk, shipstation, skuvault, smart-warehousing, stord, tlogistics and veracore. Between them, these replaced 204, 400, 404, 500, 502 and 504 responses for the same "accepted, not readable yet" case. Some code changed shape along the way:
- masonhub's `wait_for_create` / `wait_for_update` and tlogistics' `read_order_back` now take the resource and id instead of a name string.
- deposco's inbound read-back used to re-raise `ResourceNotFoundException`, which is exactly the error that makes callers retry. It now raises the new exception.

**Loop bugs fixed on the same paths:** without these, the new exception could never be raised.
- smart-warehousing (3 writes), shipmonk `create_order` and skuvault `create_receipt` never advanced their clock, so a missing record made them loop forever.
- skuvault `create_order` re-raised an earlier transient error even after the order had shown up.

**Deliberately left alone:**
- shipfusion `update_product`: shipfusion accepts the PUT but never applies it (TRA-2776), so "most likely written successfully" would be false there.
- star `cancel_order`: star ignores the cancel. The read isn't lagging.
- mirakl and overstock: these batch imports can still fail after we stop polling, so it isn't read lag.
- jazz-central: it already builds the response from the request body.
- Vendor rejection errors stay as they were.

**Knowledge:** I updated the existing gotcha "A record just created may not be readable yet" in `integration-gotchas.md` to name the exception and warn about loops whose clock never advances. I also added a rule plus a reviewer checklist item (`[BLOCK]` when violated) to `integration-patterns.md`.

**Your exception class:** I left it exactly as you wrote it. Two things to know:
- It can't be unpickled, because it has no `__reduce__` (I checked with `pickle`). Writes never go through a pickling path today, so nothing breaks now. It's a two-line add if you want it to match `RetryException`.
- Origin is still `"trackstar"`.

The PR test override should be one `-k` per integration: `yarn test -k bigcommerce -k canary7 -k controlport -k deposco -k i-fulfilment -k logicpod -k logiwa -k logiwa-io -k masonhub -k quiet -k shipfusion -k shiphero -k shipmonk -k shipstation -k skuvault -k smart-warehousing -k stord -k tlogistics -k veracore`. uv run python3 - <<'EOF'
p = ".claude/references/integration-patterns.md"
s = open(p).read()
start = s.index("- **A write whose read-back never shows the record raises")
end = s.index("\n", start) + 1
rule = """- **Only when the vendor's read lags its write: raise `WriteNotReturnedException(<Resource>(), <id>)` when the poll runs out.** Most vendors return a new record on the first read, so read it back once and add no poll or sleep. Add a short bounded poll only after seeing the lag (a read that misses a record the write just accepted, in tests or in prod). When that poll runs out, raise `utils.exceptions.WriteNotReturnedException` with the canonical resource and the id. It is a 409 saying the write most likely landed, so callers don't retry it into a duplicate. Don't raise `ResourceNotFoundException` or a 5xx there. Vendor rejections keep their own error. → `[BLOCK]` when an existing read-back poll raises anything else on timeout; a write without a poll is not a finding.
"""
s = s[:start] + rule + s[end:]
start = s.index("For each `create_*` / `update_*` / `cancel_*` that reads the record back after writing:")
end = s.index("For ID strategy:\n")
s = s[:start] + s[end:]
open(p, "w").write(s)

p = ".claude/knowledge/integration-gotchas.md"
s = open(p).read()
old = "- How to handle: poll the read-back with short sleeps over a bounded window,"
new = "- Most vendors don't do this; the first read returns the record, so don't add a poll on speculation. Only once you've seen the lag:\n- How to handle: poll the read-back with short sleeps over a bounded window,"
assert s.count(old) == 1
open(p, "w").write(s.replace(old, new))
EOF

This is the one documented exception to "hoist stateless helpers to module level": auth stays together, in the class, around the request helper. Don't intermix them with the framework install/identity defaults (a separate cluster above), and don't drop them to module level below the class.

When extracted, it lives at the very bottom of the file, **after every `format_*` function** — never before or interleaved with them.  - **No raise-only method stubs for unsupported flows.** An integration never ships a data or write method whose body only raises. Omit the method entirely — the framework's `is_implemented` treats an absent method and a raise-only body identically, so the stub is dead lines that read as intent. content.content: - How to handle: most vendors return the record on the first read, so don't add a poll on speculation. Once you've seen the lag, poll the read-back with short sleeps over a bounded window, and make sure the loop's clock actually advances (a `current_time` that is never updated spins forever). On running out, format from what the create itself returned, or raise `WriteNotReturnedException(<Resource>(), <id>)` from `utils/exceptions.py`. It is a 409 saying the write most likely landed and will show up on the next sync, so callers don't retry into a duplicate. Never raise `ResourceNotFoundException` or a 5xx there; those are the signals callers retry on. The same applies to an update or cancel whose change hasn't shown up in the read yet. shipfusion and skuvault are worked examples.

lines: - Vendors with async write pipelines accept a create and then answer the detail/list read with an empty result for seconds to minutes — often as `200` with "no records" / `items: []`, not a 404. Presence of the record's id field in the read body, not the create's status code, is the readiness signal.

- When it bites: a create whose immediate read-back raises not-found invites a duplicate-creating retry (by the caller or a retry layer), or the formatted create response gets built from the empty read and drops fields. Sandboxes typically lag less than prod, so tests stay green while prod duplicates.

When writing a rule into `.claude/references/integration-patterns.md` or `integration-gotchas.md` from a fix that touched some integrations, scope it to the situation that triggers it. Don't phrase it so every integration must adopt the mechanism.

**Why:** for TRA-2952 (WriteNotReturnedException), I first wrote the patterns rule and a reviewer checklist item that read as "every write must poll its read-back". The user pushed back: most vendors return the record on the first read, and a universal rule would push writers and reviewers to add speculative polls.

**How to apply:** lead with "only when X is observed", say what the default is when it isn't, and make sure reviewer `[BLOCK]` items can't fire on integrations that don't have the problem.

content.text:
You were right: the old rule read like every write should poll its read-back. I've narrowed both docs so a poll is only added once the lag has actually been seen.

- **`integration-patterns.md`**: the rule now starts "Only when the vendor's read lags its write". Most vendors return the record on the first read, so the default is to read it back once with no poll or sleep. The `[BLOCK]` now applies only to an existing poll that raises something other than `WriteNotReturnedException` when it runs out. It also says outright that a write without a poll is not a finding. I removed the reviewer-checklist item entirely, because it read as "every write must have a bounded poll".
- **`integration-gotchas.md`**: "How to handle" now opens by saying most vendors don't lag, so don't add a poll on speculation. The guidance on polling and the exception only applies once you've seen the lag.

The integration changes are unaffected. Each of those 19 integrations already had a read-back poll, or a single read for a vendor known to lag, before this branch. I only changed what they raise when it runs out, and fixed the loops that never advanced their clock. I also saved this as a feedback memory, so future rules I add will be scoped to where the problem actually happens.

content.text:
`id` is now optional, and each call site passes the `id` the integration actually returns, or nothing. You were right about canary7: `format_inbound_shipment` uses `shipment["id"]`, and so did about a third of the other call sites. I'd been passing a reference number those integrations don't use as the id.

**The exception:** `WriteNotReturnedException(resource, id=None)`. With no id the message reads "The modified Order did not come back…", and with one it's "The modified Order 123 did not come back…".

**Id dropped, because only the vendor's own id is the Trackstar id and we don't have it when the read-back fails:**
- canary7, deposco, logicpod, logiwa, smart-warehousing and veracore inbound shipments
- logicpod product, and the logicpod, i-fulfilment, smart-warehousing and deposco customer orders
- masonhub creates of inbound shipments, orders and returns (the cid isn't the id)
- smart-warehousing return
- skuvault inbound create (its id is `PoId`, not the PO number)

**Id corrected to the real one:**
- quiet: `{order_number}_{warehouse}`
- shipfusion `create_order`: the `orderNumber` we send. `update_order` uses the path `item_id`.
- shipmonk `create_return`: `rma`. I dropped the now-unused `created_return_id` and `response`.
- skuvault `create_receipt`: the inbound `item_id`
- deposco `cancel_customer_order`: the path `order_id`

The deposco customer-order sites also use `Order()` now instead of `DeposcoCustomerOrder()`, because the customer called an order endpoint. The rest (bigcommerce, controlport, logiwa-io, masonhub updates and product, shiphero, shipmonk orders, shipstation, skuvault product/kit/order, stord, tlogistics, shipfusion product/inbound/return) already passed the real id, so I left them alone.

**Tests:** I reran the write tests for masonhub, shipmonk, shipfusion, quiet and deposco: 18 passed and 2 failed. Both failures are shipfusion (`test_create_product`, `test_create_order`), and both still failed when I reran them alone. In each, the sandbox didn't return the new record within the 20s poll, so the new exception fired with the right id. That's the same timeout that made `test_create_product` fail once earlier (it passed on retry). I didn't check main, but it has the same 20s poll and would fail here with its old 404. I didn't touch the tests or the poll window.

Lint, imports and formatting all check out. Nothing is committed yet.

content.text:
I removed it only because it became unused. Before this change, `created_return_id` was read in one place: the old error message. Once that error switched to `rma`, ruff flagged it as an unused variable (F841), so I deleted the assignment, and `response` went with it.

I passed `rma` rather than the vendor's id because `format_return` uses `return_id = return_["rma"]` (`integrations/wms/shipmonk/integration.py`). That's the id customers know the return by, so it belongs in the message.

You're right that the cleanup cost more than it was worth:
- **Diff noise.** It changes lines the fix didn't need to touch.
- **A lost loud failure.** `response["data"]["id"]` raised a `KeyError` if the create came back without that shape. Now an unexpected create response falls straight through to the 20s poll and ends as a `WriteNotReturnedException`, which tells the customer the write probably landed when it may not have.

I'd restore those two lines exactly as they were and accept the new F841. Or, if you want the vendor's id visible, `WriteNotReturnedException(Return(), rma)` could be preceded by a log of `created_return_id`, though that adds code for little benefit. Should I restore them?

lines: - Vendors with async write pipelines accept a create and then answer the detail/list read with an empty result for seconds to minutes — often as `200` with "no records" / `items: []`, not a 404. Presence of the record's id field in the read body, not the create's status code, is the readiness signal.

- When it bites: a create whose immediate read-back raises not-found invites a duplicate-creating retry (by the caller or a retry layer), or the formatted create response gets built from the empty read and drops fields. Sandboxes typically lag less than prod, so tests stay green while prod duplicates.

-- How to handle: most vendors return the record on the first read, so don't add a poll on speculation. Once you've seen the lag, poll the read-back with short sleeps over a bounded window, and make sure the loop's clock actually advances (a `current_time` that is never updated spins forever). On running out, format from what the create itself returned, or raise `WriteNotReturnedException(<Resource>(), <id>)` from `utils/exceptions.py`. It is a 409 saying the write most likely landed and will show up on the next sync, so callers don't retry into a duplicate. Never raise `ResourceNotFoundException` or a 5xx there; those are the signals callers retry on. The same applies to an update or cancel whose change hasn't shown up in the read yet. shipfusion and skuvault are worked examples.

I've fixed two of Greptile's three findings locally. The idempotency one needs your call before I touch shared API code. Nothing is committed or pushed.

**1. Idempotency key lets a same-key retry write twice (P1). Valid; your decision.** `api_write_resource` deletes the key row on any exception (`utils/api.py:1311`). So when the customer retries with the same `Idempotency-Key` after a `WriteNotReturnedException`, the write goes to the vendor again. Today's 500s and 504s had the same gap. The difference is that this error now says the write probably landed, which makes deleting the key the wrong move.

There are two ways to fix it:
- **A. Don't delete the key on this exception (my pick).** It's a one-line `except WriteNotReturnedException: raise` before the generic delete. The row stays `in_progress`, so a same-key retry gets the existing 409 ("still in progress"), which is safe. After 15 minutes (`IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_STILL_RUNNING_SECONDS`), `create_idempotency_key_row` treats it as a dead request and runs the write again. By then most lagging records have synced, but that isn't guaranteed.
- **B. Add a third row status, e.g. `not_returned`.** A same-key retry for the key's 24h lifetime would then get this same 409 back instead of a second write. It's airtight, but it adds a new status, plus handling in `use_idempotency_key` and tests.

**2. smart-warehousing poll can still spin forever (P1). Valid, my bug, fixed.** My earlier fix only advanced the clock when the outer `Receipts` / `order_details` key was missing. If the key is present but its value is null, the loop never advances. All three polls now sleep and advance whenever nothing has been found yet.

**3. logicpod read-back error leaves out the id (P2). Partly valid, fixed for product only.** The product create returns `new_product_id`, and `format_product` uses `item["id"]`, which the read-back compares against `new_product_id`. So that is the real id, and I'd wrongly dropped it. For inbound shipments and orders, the only identifiers available are the PO and order numbers, not the id `format_*` returns, so those correctly stay without one.

Greptile read the patterns rule as "always pass an id", which is why it called this a merge blocker. I reworded the rule and the gotcha: pass the id only when it's the exact value `format_*` returns as `id`.

resource: Resource = resource_type(integration)
    action: Action = action_type(resource)

    body = parse_request_body()
    tag_write_function(action)
    loaded_body, unused_fields = validate_write_body(integration, action, body)
    idempotency_key, replay = use_idempotency_key(loaded_body, resource)
    if replay is not None:
        return replay
    write_args = (resource, action, body, loaded_body, unused_fields, fail_validation)
    try:
        if action.is_batch():
            to_return = write_items(*write_args)
        else:
            to_return = write_item(*write_args, item_id)
    except Exception:
        delete_idempotency_key(idempotency_key)
        raise
    store_response_for_replay(idempotency_key, action, to_return)
    return to_return

# Code style (pokedex Python)

The always-on subset, consolidated from CLAUDE.md and `integration-patterns.md` "Code style". Full reviewer checklist (incl. advisory / new-build-only items like `while True`, guard clauses, inline dict values): `.claude/references/integration-patterns.md` "Code style".

- **No docstrings, with two exceptions.** Pokedex code is self-documenting. Both exceptions are where the docstring is published text, not a comment: `api.py` endpoint handlers, whose docstring is the endpoint's OpenAPI summary and description (the rollout pushes that spec to Mintlify and Svix, so it is the public API docs, and every public endpoint carries one); Alembic migration modules under `migrations/versions/`, which keep the generated header (title, `Revision ID`, `Revises`, `Create Date`) plus a line of rationale when the schema change is not obvious from the operations. Nothing under `integrations/`, `utils/`, `resources/`, or `actions/` has one.
- **Default to no comment; when in doubt, delete.** A comment exists only when the change is not obvious from the code alone. If the code, a variable name, or the error message beside it already says it, the comment is noise — delete it rather than polish it. That covers narration ("sum the quantities per sku"), section labels, and anything restating an assert or a raise.
- **Comments: lowercase, ≤2 lines, why not what.** Vendor quirks, surprising invariants, non-obvious couplings. Vendor field names keep their original casing inside a lowercase comment (`DeliveryNotes` stays `DeliveryNotes`) — lowercasing them breaks the reference. The ceiling yields only when a genuinely non-obvious vendor data model or a disambiguating example needs the room and nothing shorter carries it. The same ceiling applies to raised error messages — a `PokedexException` says what went wrong and what to do in a line or two, not a paragraph.
- **ELI5, no jargon.** Write it the way you'd say it out loud to an engineer new to the codebase: plain words any SWE understands cold, in one read. No noun-stacks ("multi-lot pick collision"), no arrow chains (`x → y → z`), no model-speak ("ensure correctness", "for clarity", "leverage"), no clever compression that needs decoding ("must not look like it did"). "with no batch number, picks from different batches get combined here, so we can't keep a single expiry date" beats "blank-batch multi-lot picks collapse under the package uniqueness key, dropping the expiry anchor".
- **Comments are self-contained.** Never reference `api-summary.md`, any `.claude/...` file, doctrine vocabulary ("tier-3", "shallow-fix", "per integration-patterns"), or the authoring agent. A reader at HEAD with only this file open must understand it.
- **Comments never name** customer orgs, the source integration a pattern was copied from, or observation dates — those leak or rot. The ban is on customers: naming the integration's own vendor inside its own files is normal. Rich rationale (customer, pattern source, load-bearing dates) lives in `api-summary.md` "Field-mapping decisions". Exception: vendor/3PL support-contact lines inside `support()` — naming contacts is that method's job.
- **Raise, don't `assert`.** Runtime error paths raise `PokedexException` (or the typed `create_*` exception helpers), never `assert` — asserts strip under `python -O` and carry no status or origin. `assert` belongs in tests only.
- **A package `__init__.py` that re-exports lists those names in `__all__`.** Re-exports are the point of the file, but every one of them reads as an unused import to the linter, so the list is what keeps it quiet and doubles as the package's public surface. Add a name in both places or the linter flags it again.
- **No `@property` on anything a subclass overrides.** A value an integration can change is a plain method, so every call site shows it's dispatched rather than read off the instance. `@property` is still fine for something defined once and never overridden (`staging_key`, `bucket`). Name a boolean method for how it reads at the call site — `uses_browserbase()`, not `use_browserbase()`.
- **No `ABC` / `@abstractmethod`.** A base class declares a method subclasses must supply by raising `NotImplementedError` in the body, with a short message saying what the subclass owes. That's the one pattern used everywhere else, and on integrations it's load-bearing: `BaseIntegration.is_implemented` reads a method's source looking for that raise to decide which functions an integration supports, so an abstract stub would be read as implemented and get scheduled.
- **UPPER_CASE names are module-level only.** A constant-style value scoped inside a function is a lowercase local like any other; capitals are reserved for module-level constants (status maps, page sizes, vendor tunables).
- **No leading-underscore "private" names** on methods, attributes, or locals. Underscore privacy isn't enforced here and signals nothing. If a class helper needs `self` it's a method; if not, hoist it module-level; if used once, inline it. (Dunders like `__init__` are exempt.)
- **Error-driven: avoid `.get()` — on vendor-response reads.** Loud failures (a `KeyError` during `yarn crawl`) are how we learn real API behavior. `.get(field, default)` on a vendor response is allowed only after observing the field is genuinely sometimes-absent. Nullable is not optional: a key the vendor always sends but sometimes nulls is read with a direct index (plus an `or` fallback when a default is needed) — `.get()` there misstates the contract by implying the key can be missing. The rule does not cover reads where absence is the normal, documented case — optional fields of a validated write payload in `create_*`/`update_*` methods, marshmallow `query_data` in API handlers (absent optional params are omitted from the dict), and our own state attributes that most rows don't carry — there `.get()` is the convention and is self-documenting. Comment a `.get()` only when the absence is surprising (the contract says the field should be there and observation proved otherwise: `# vendor returns null for unfulfilled orders`); a `.get()` on a documented-optional field needs no comment.
- **No list/dict comprehensions in integration code.** Use multi-line `for` loops with named intermediates — comprehensions are opaque under `pdb`.
- **No `logger.info` / `print` in integration code** (carrier is the documented exception — its async/queued flows justify checkpoint logging). Every other type stays quiet: Datadog spans + connection-error rows are the observability surface; `logger.warning`/`error` only for genuinely surprising, actionable states.
- **Platform constants live in `config.py`.** Feature modules `import config`; don't scatter `os.environ.get`. Integration-level constants (status maps, page sizes, vendor base URLs, per-vendor tunables) stay in the integration's own module — they're hard to unify across vendors and don't belong in the shared config.
- **Favor simplicity over cleverness — and the smallest fix that addresses the root cause.** A fix that adds new mechanisms (a helper, a wrapper, a retry layer, config) where editing an existing line suffices is overengineered and gets rejected in review. Before inventing a new shape, check how neighboring integrations already solve the same problem and match it. The same bar applies to edge cases: a narrow race or double-failure edge that self-corrects on the next cycle (or whose outcome is still correct for the user) is documented — or made observable with a log line — not engineered around with new state machines or guards.

- **Reuse the codebase's words; never coin a verb.** A name is found, not composed: before naming a function, helper, constant, status value, or table, grep for how neighbors name the same operation on the same kind of thing (`rg -n 'def \w+_<noun>\b'`, `rg -n 'def \w+_row\b'`) and pick from the verbs that come back; the search is by object, never by a list of verbs, because a list is itself a vocabulary that drifts. Dynamo row helpers are `create_ / get_ / update_ / store_ / delete_<thing>_row`. Under `integrations/`, data-function and action names come from the resource and action contracts, so there is nothing to choose. A status string is the word the API's error text uses for that state (`unconfirmed` when the 409 says "could not be confirmed"), so the row, the log line, and the error read the same. A word from one recent feature is not established vocabulary; count its uses across the repo before adopting it. Payments, ops, and distributed-systems jargon (`settle`, `claim`, `release`, `landed`, `in flight`, `ambiguous`, `reconcile`) is a coined verb here unless the grep shows it already carries that meaning in this codebase. Say what the code does in words the code already uses: `mark_<row>_succeeded`, `store_write_ids_for_replay`, `write_may_have_reached_vendor`.
- **Comments and error messages use the code's own names.** A comment names the function, status, and field exactly as the code spells them and describes the mechanism in the same verbs. A comment that introduces a second vocabulary for the thing beside it is rewritten in the code's words or deleted.

## Running code & tests
- **Tests: only `yarn test` with filters.** Never `python -m pytest` or raw `pytest`. Scopes/markers: `.claude/skills/run-scripts/guides/test.md`.
- **Ad-hoc Python: `uv run python3`.** Never raw `python3`/`python` — dependencies resolve through `uv`.

    checked = 0

        header_names = []

It hits only pages full of orders that were changed at the same moment, and at 1000 per page the crawl retried the same page every hour without moving. A smaller page loads the same orders, so nothing is skipped. This is a time limit on Extensiv's query, like deposco's maximum request duration, not a bug or outage, so Extensiv support was not contacted.

- Evidence: conn `1fa88f45295a4289b16dfc8a6488b8f3`, 2026-09-22. About 1,050 orders were all modified at 13:01–13:02 (Extensiv time), and three hourly crawls failed on that page. From that cursor, `detail=All` took 4.7s at 250 and 32.9s at 500, and timed out at 1000. A 1000-order page from 13:22 took 9.3s, and one from a later 656-order burst at 14:55 took 11.3s. The prod pass with this change timed out at 1000 on page 1, loaded it at 500, then loaded pages 2–7 at 1000 (5,531 orders). No Linear ticket: shipping-tree and deposco already shrink their page when the vendor times out, so this is not an anti-pattern here.

-- `create_order_shipment` — `confirm_order` (Extensiv-only write field, default `true`). When `false`, we set package tracking and the order's routing (carrier, mode, pickup date, tracking) and skip `POST orders/confirmer`, so the order stays open. `confirm_date` and `shipping_cost` are rejected when `confirm_order` is `false`, because Extensiv only takes them on the confirm call. The schema also sets `skip_retrieval` itself when `confirm_order` is `false`, and the response is just `{success, id}`: an open order has no shipments (`format_order` builds them only once the order is closed), so the shipment endpoint's response checks would log three errors on every call. The routing rejection stays swallowed as it always was, so with `confirm_order: false` the call reports success even when only `tracking_number` was sent and nothing changed.
